# Why R²D Is Not Coarse-Graining

R<sup>2</sup>D can initially sound like coarse-graining.

Many subordinate realizations correspond to one readable enclosing state.

Fine-scale distinctions become unreadable from a larger boundary.

Detailed paths can cease to be recoverable from the enclosing description.

Those features resemble familiar ideas from statistical mechanics,
renormalization, effective theory, and information reduction.

But R<sup>2</sup>D makes a different claim.

> **Coarse-graining usually changes the description of an already-defined
> state. R<sup>2</sup>D changes the count boundary that defines what the state
> is.**

The distinction is between

$$
\boxed{
\text{less detail about the same state}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\text{a different state domain}.
}
$$

[Boundaries Define Scientific Objects →](boundaries.qmd)

## The Familiar Coarse-Graining Picture

A conventional coarse-graining procedure often begins with a detailed state

$$
x
$$

in some underlying state space.

A map then assigns many detailed states to one coarser description:

$$
x
\longmapsto
X.
$$

The detailed states remain mathematically defined underneath the reduced
description.

The observer or model simply retains fewer distinctions.

Schematically,

$$
\boxed{
\text{detailed state}
\rightarrow
\text{reduced description of that state}.
}
$$

This is enormously useful.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not dispute it.

The question is whether this operation is primitive enough to explain why
the original state was a **microstate** in the first place.

## R<sup>2</sup>D Starts One Step Earlier

At boundary \(B_n\), R<sup>2</sup>D defines a formal microstate as one
compatible joint realization of the immediately subordinate peer boundaries:

$$
\mu_n
\in
\mathfrak M_n.
$$

The boundary then classifies those realizations through

$$
\pi_n:
\mathfrak M_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal M_n.
$$

A readable macrostate is

$$
i
=
\pi_n(\mu_n).
$$

Thus neither "microstate" nor "macrostate" is assigned independently of the
boundary.

They are boundary-relative categories.

[Macrostate and Microstate →](macrostate-microstate.qmd)

## Change the Boundary, Change the Domain

Now change from

$$
B_n
$$

to

$$
B_{n+1}.
$$

The enclosing boundary defines its own formal microstate domain

$$
\mathfrak M_{n+1}
$$

and its own readable macrostate domain

$$
\mathcal M_{n+1}.
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D does not assume a boundary-independent identity map such that

$$
\mathfrak M_n
\equiv
\mathfrak M_{n+1}
$$

or

$$
\mathcal M_n
\equiv
\mathcal M_{n+1}.
$$

Instead,

$$
\boxed{
B_n\rightarrow B_{n+1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{new count domain}.
}
$$

And therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{new count domain}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{new state identity}.
}
$$

This is recursive replacement.

[Recursive Replacement →](recursive-replacement.qmd)

## The Difference Is Not Merely Resolution

Suppose a transition

$$
i\rightarrow k
$$

is readable as a macrostate transition at subordinate boundary

$$
B_{n-1,\alpha}.
$$

Relative to the enclosing boundary \(B_n\), that same physical realization
has microstate meaning.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{macrostate transition at }B_{n-1,\alpha}
=
\text{microstate transition relative to }B_n.
}
$$

If the observer wants to resolve the transition directly, the observer must
move back to the boundary where it has macrostate meaning.

So increased resolution does not merely reveal a hidden microstate while
leaving its classification unchanged.

It changes the count boundary.

And that changes what kind of state the transition is.

## A Microstate Is Not an Absolute Underlying Object

This is the conceptual break.

In an ordinary coarse-graining picture, one may imagine a fully specified
microscopic state existing underneath every larger-scale description.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not require such an absolute microstate classification.

A state is a microstate **relative to a particular boundary**.

Change the boundary, and the word "microstate" refers to a different
relationship.

Thus:

> **Microstate is not a synonym for smallest object.**

> **Macrostate is not a synonym for largest object.**

They are count relations.

## Many-to-One Classification Is Not Yet the Difference

The classification map

$$
\pi_n:
\mathfrak M_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal M_n
$$

is generally many-to-one.

For macrostate \(i\),

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
$$

Many formal microstates belong to one macrostate.

This mathematical structure certainly resembles coarse-graining.

But the many-to-one map is not, by itself, what distinguishes R<sup>2</sup>D.

The stronger claim appears when the boundary changes.

At the next boundary, the old state classification does not simply remain
the hidden primitive state beneath a reduced description.

A new state domain is defined.

That is recursive replacement.

## The Coin Example Makes the Difference Concrete

Take ten coins.

At the single-coin boundary, the readable states are

$$
H
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T.
$$

At the ten-coin boundary, the readable state might instead be

$$
N_H=0,1,\ldots,10.
$$

The ensemble macrostate

$$
N_H=6
$$

has multiplicity

$$
W_{n,6}
=
\binom{10}{6}.
$$

One might describe this as coarse-graining over individual coin identities.

That description is mathematically useful.

But now take the next recursive step.

Suppose ten such ensemble boundaries become the immediately subordinate
peers of \(B_{n+1}\).

R<sup>2</sup>D says \(B_{n+1}\) counts **ten already-defined ensemble
landscapes**.

It does not restore one hundred individual \(H/T\) identities as the
primitive readable states of the new boundary.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
10\text{ coin states}
\rightarrow
1\text{ ensemble landscape}
\rightarrow
1\text{ enclosing landscape}.
}
$$

Each step defines a new count domain.

[The Coins Example →](coins.qmd)

## A Closed-Form Result Does Not Restore the Lower Ontology

The enclosing multiplicity may sometimes be simplified into a familiar
closed-form expression.

For example, recursive composition can recover the same combinatorial total
that would be obtained by directly counting one hundred binary elements.

That equality is mathematically important.

But it does not imply that the one hundred individual coin identities have
become the primitive readable states at the enclosing boundary.

The equality concerns **count consequence**.

It does not establish **identity persistence**.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{same multiplicity result}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{same state ontology}.
}
$$

This distinction becomes important far beyond the coin example.

## What Is Replaced?

When the count boundary changes, several identities need not persist as the
same readable objects.

A subordinate:

- state,
- transition,
- source identity,
- or internal path

can remain consequential without remaining readable under the same
classification.

The important relation is therefore not

$$
\boxed{
\text{same object}
\rightarrow
\text{less information}.
}
$$

It is

$$
\boxed{
\text{subordinate count identity}
\rightarrow
\text{recursive replacement}
\rightarrow
\text{enclosing count identity}.
}
$$

## What Is Preserved?

Recursive replacement does not imply that everything disappears.

What can persist is the **recursive relation**.

A completed local closure

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
$$

can remain related to an enclosing occurrence

$$
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

But

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\not\equiv
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
}
$$

They are different boundary-defined count objects.

Recursive carry expresses their relationship:

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
}
$$

The path identity is replaced.

The recursive relation remains consequential.

[Recursive Carry →](recursive-carry.qmd)

## Unreadable Does Not Mean Destroyed

This is another important distinction.

Suppose the enclosing boundary does not preserve the identity of the local
peer or its internal path.

That does not mean the local path was destroyed.

It remains definable at the boundary where it was readable.

It has simply ceased to possess the same count meaning from the new boundary.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{unreadable from }B_{n+1}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{nonexistent at }B_n.
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore does not replace reductionism with a claim that
smaller-scale structures are unreal.

It makes their identity boundary relative.

## Information Loss Is Not the Primitive Operation

The language of information loss can also obscure the distinction.

One might say that moving to \(B_{n+1}\) "loses information" about the
subordinate realization.

That may be a useful description from the perspective of an observer who
wants to reconstruct the lower-boundary path.

But R<sup>2</sup>D does not take that loss as primitive.

The primitive statement is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{the new boundary defines a different count domain}.
}
$$

Failure to reconstruct the previous path is then a consequence of the new
classification.

The ontology changes first.

The recoverability changes with it.

## The Enclosing State Is Not an Incomplete Lower State

This changes how a macrostate should be interpreted.

The enclosing macrostate is not merely an incomplete report about a more
fundamental subordinate macrostate.

It is a state defined by a different classification.

Thus:

> **A macrostate is not merely a lossy microstate.**

And:

> **A microstate is not merely a more detailed macrostate.**

They belong to different boundary-relative relations.

## Renormalization Is an Important Precedent

Renormalization provides a powerful example of scale-dependent scientific
description.

Under renormalization, variables and couplings can change as the scale of
description changes.

Degrees of freedom that are explicit at one scale need not remain explicit
at another.

R<sup>2</sup>D treats this as an important mathematical and conceptual
precedent.

But its starting question is different.

Renormalization generally asks:

> **Given a state description, how does its effective representation change
> with scale?**

R<sup>2</sup>D asks:

> **What makes a state micro or macro before that scale transformation is
> performed?**

Its answer is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{the count boundary}.
}
$$

## Effective Theory Is Also a Precedent

Effective theories likewise show that not every lower-scale degree of
freedom must remain explicit in a useful higher-level description.

Their residual effects may instead appear through effective parameters or
interactions.

R<sup>2</sup>D is compatible with the practical usefulness of this approach.

Its stronger claim is that the issue is not only which variables remain
useful.

The state categories themselves are boundary indexed.

Therefore the scale transformation can alter what qualifies as the object
being described.

## Emergence Is Not Enough Either

R<sup>2</sup>D is also related to familiar ideas of emergence.

Larger-scale systems can display organizing principles not obvious from
inspection of isolated components.

But the R<sup>2</sup>D claim is more specific than

> "the whole is more than the sum of its parts."

It identifies a proposed mathematical reason:

$$
\boxed{
\text{changing the count boundary changes what is being counted}.
}
$$

The enclosing state is a classification of compatible subordinate
realizations.

Its multiplicity belongs to that classification.

Its directional possibility depends on compatibility with a still enclosing
domain.

Thus the recursive architecture is specified mathematically rather than
introduced only as a general philosophical notion of emergence.

## Direction Makes the Distinction Even Stronger

The difference from ordinary coarse-graining becomes sharper when direction
is introduced.

Suppose the local multiplicity landscape remains fixed:

$$
\mathcal W_n
=
\{W_{n,i}\}.
$$

Now change the enclosing compatibility relation.

The local possibility difference

$$
\Delta P_{n,i\rightarrow k}
$$

can change.

It can vanish.

It can increase.

It can reverse sign.

All without changing the native local multiplicities.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{same local state space}
+
\text{different enclosing compatibility}
\rightarrow
\text{different directional support}.
}
$$

This is not simply information removal.

It is a new across-boundary count relation.

[Possibility →](possibility.qmd)

## Constraint Adds Another Enclosing Relation

Likewise, changing the enclosing productive constraint changes

$$
\Delta R
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}\lambda_n.
$$

Therefore the local asymmetry

$$
\Delta A
=
\Delta P-\Delta R
$$

can change while the native multiplicity landscape remains fixed.

So the local realized state depends not merely on how much subordinate
information is retained.

It depends on relations defined by the enclosing boundary.

[Constraint and Retention →](constraint-retention.qmd)

## Coarse-Graining Does Not Automatically Specify Causality

This distinction matters because coarse-graining itself need not make any
claim about causal priority.

It may simply be a mathematical transformation used to construct an
effective description.

R<sup>2</sup>D adds a separate causal proposal:

$$
\boxed{
\text{enclosing relation organizes}
\Longrightarrow
\text{subordinate mechanism realizes}.
}
$$

That causal inversion does not follow merely from the fact that a description
is coarse-grained.

It follows from the additional R<sup>2</sup>D architecture of boundary-defined
multiplicity, enclosing compatibility, possibility, constraint, and local
realization.

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

## Readability Loss Is Not an Error

A boundary cannot read every relation simultaneously.

A subordinate transition may be individually unreadable from an enclosing
boundary.

An enclosing relation may likewise be unavailable from a subordinate
boundary.

This is simply a **readability limit**.

It is not automatically a theoretical error.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{unreadable}
\neq
\text{incorrect}.
}
$$

A boundary-specific theory can accurately describe what remains readable.

## Readability Limit Is Not EP Projection

R<sup>2</sup>D distinguishes a readability limit from what it calls
**epiphenomenological projection**, or EP projection.

A readability limit asks:

> **What can be directly resolved from this boundary?**

An EP projection makes an additional causal inference:

> **Because only this consequence is readable, it must be the primitive
> cause.**

The latter does not follow from the former.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{readability limit}
\neq
\text{EP projection}.
}
$$

An effective or coarse-grained theory can therefore be useful and accurate
without committing an EP projection.

The proposed error occurs only when an omitted recursive relation is replaced
by primitive causal agency assigned to one of its readable consequences.

## A Model Can Be Effective Without Being Ontologically Primitive

This gives R<sup>2</sup>D a way to preserve successful science.

A model can:

- predict observations;
- identify useful effective variables;
- compress inaccessible detail;
- and correctly describe correlations

without proving that its state variables are the primitive objects of nature.

That distinction is especially important across scientific scales.

Predictive success and primitive ontology are different questions.

## Three Different Questions

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore separates three questions.

### What is readable?

The count boundary determines this.

### What mathematics describes the readable relation?

The domain-specific scientific theory answers this.

### What organizes that relation?

This is the causal question addressed by recursive counting.

Confusing the three creates unnecessary ontological commitments.

Keeping them separate allows a scientific model to remain completely useful
within its proper boundary.

## The R<sup>2</sup>D Difference in One Diagram

The ordinary coarse-graining picture can be represented as

$$
\boxed{
\text{underlying detailed state}
\rightarrow
\text{reduced representation of that state}.
}
$$

The R<sup>2</sup>D architecture is

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{state domain at }B_n
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{completed realization}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{change of count boundary}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{new state domain at }B_{n+1}
\end{array}
}
$$

What survives is not necessarily an unchanged lower-boundary state.

What survives is the recursively organized relation.

## The Strongest Statement

The difference can be summarized in one sentence:

> **Coarse-graining asks what happens when detail is removed from a state
> description. R<sup>2</sup>D asks what happens when the boundary defining
> the state itself changes.**

That is why recursive replacement is not simply another name for
coarse-graining.

It begins one logical step earlier.

---

## Core Relations

### Boundary-relative classification

$$
\boxed{
\pi_n:
\mathfrak M_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal M_n
}
$$

### Boundary change

$$
\boxed{
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathcal M_n
\not\equiv
\mathcal M_{n+1}
}
$$

### Change in transition meaning

$$
\boxed{
\text{macrostate transition at }B_{n-1,\alpha}
=
\text{microstate transition relative to }B_n
}
$$

### Recursive replacement

$$
\boxed{
\text{state identity changes while recursive consequence can remain}
}
$$

### Recursive carry

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

### Distinct boundary-specific objects

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\not\equiv
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

---

## The Key Distinction

R<sup>2</sup>D does not claim that coarse-graining is mathematically wrong.

It makes a different ontological proposal.

> **The subordinate state is not merely hidden.**

> **Its boundary-defined identity has been replaced.**

> **The enclosing state is not merely a blurrier version of the same
> object.**

> **It belongs to a new count domain.**

> **What can persist across the change is the recursive relation, not an
> unchanged state identity.**

That distinction leads directly to the R<sup>2</sup>D concept of scientific
objecthood.
